16:9 horizontal composition, flat pure white background, featuring only a thick hand-drawn ornamental frame running continuously around all four edges, leaving a large completely empty white rectangular space in the center. The frame is built entirely from intertwined stylized algae and seaweed forms, illustrated in a playful naive editorial graphic style: long curling fronds, broad ribbon-like kelp leaves, soft branching algae, rounded lobes, looping tendrils, wavy organic blades, spiraling tips, overlapping marine plant shapes and irregular hand-drawn silhouettes that weave into one another like a living border. Main color is a rich saturated green covering most of the algae forms, with bold vivid red used sparingly as small accent elements: round berry-like dots, tiny circular nodes, occasional small algae tips and isolated graphic details distributed rhythmically around the frame. Thick imperfect black outlines around every shape, slightly uneven hand-inked contours, simple flat color fills with no gradients, no shading, no texture rendering, no dimensional lighting. The algae should feel whimsical, abstract and decorative rather than scientifically accurate, with exaggerated curling gestures, irregular asymmetry and a loose hand-drawn rhythm. Some seaweed shapes overlap and interlock, creating dense clusters at the corners and slightly thinner sections along the middle of each edge. The frame should feel handmade, playful, slightly psychedelic and reminiscent of independent magazine illustration, risograph-inspired graphic art and vintage underground editorial drawing. Preserve visible white gaps between some intertwined forms so the border feels airy rather than like a solid block. The center must remain completely blank and untouched, with absolutely no people, photography, text, objects or illustrations inside it. Crisp flat white background, green-dominant algae border, red accents, bold black linework, highly graphic 2D illustration, 16:9 aspect ratio.

horizontal composition, flat warm cream background, featuring only a bold ornamental graphic frame around all four edges, leaving a large completely empty rectangular opening in the center for future imagery. The border is inspired by vintage printed packaging, old travel ephemera, hand-screen-printed posters and decorative African/roadside sign graphics, but reinterpreted as a contemporary editorial frame about courage, confidence and forward movement. Use a very limited two-color palette: rich burnt orange as the dominant color, with soft warm cream as the contrasting accent and negative space. Optional thin dark-orange linework only—no extra colors.
The frame is highly structured and geometric rather than floral: long rectangular side panels, repeating stripes, chevrons, diamonds, arrows, zigzags, parallel lines, small grids, sunburst motifs, simplified road markings and decorative symmetrical patterns. The four corners contain larger illustrated medallions or sign-like graphic elements, while the horizontal top and bottom sections feel like vintage banner strips. Everything is outlined with slightly imperfect hand-drawn lines, subtle analogue printing irregularities, slightly misregistered ink, screen-print texture and a tactile vintage graphic quality. Keep the design flat and two-dimensional with absolutely no gradients, photorealism, shadows or 3D effects.
Integrate simplified illustrated road signs as symbols of courage and self-belief directly into the ornamentation: an upward-pointing arrow, a winding-road sign suggesting perseverance, a steep-climb sign representing challenge, a crossroads sign representing choice, a forward-only arrow, a small destination flag, a rising sun over a road, and a stylized road disappearing toward the horizon. Treat these as charming hand-drawn pictograms rather than realistic traffic signage. Repeat small arrowheads, directional markers and abstract road lanes as decorative filler throughout the border.
At the center of the top frame, prominently incorporate the large title “I CAN DO IT”, set in bold hand-drawn uppercase lettering integrated into a decorative banner panel. The lettering should feel confident, slightly quirky and handmade, with imperfect vintage typography rather than a clean digital font. Make this the strongest textual element of the border.
Scatter additional small motivational words and micro-phrases throughout the side panels, medallions, corners and bottom banner, primarily functioning as graphic texture rather than readable paragraphs. Include phrases such as “KEEP GOING”, “TRUST YOURSELF”, “BE BRAVE”, “FORWARD”, “NO FEAR”, “GO FURTHER”, “TAKE THE ROAD”, “YOU GOT THIS”, “ONE MORE STEP”, “COURAGE”, “BELIEVE”, “MOVE”, “YES”, “RISE”, “TRY AGAIN”, and “KEEP MOVING.” Mix tiny uppercase text, condensed lettering, curved text inside circular badges, abbreviated initials, numbers, arrows and fragmented typographic marks so that much of the writing behaves like visual texture on an old printed object.
The vertical left and right borders should be dense and rhythmic, combining long repeating road-lane patterns with small signs, tiny words, diamonds, arrows and geometric symbols. Top and bottom borders should be broader and more elaborate, containing the principal banners, directional chevrons and ornamental typography. Corners can contain quarter-circle medallions with miniature road/horizon illustrations and words like COURAGE, FORWARD, RISE, or YES.
Maintain a charming handmade imperfection: rough ink edges, uneven line weight, tiny registration errors, subtle halftone grain, slightly distressed screen-print marks and irregular spacing, while still feeling intentionally designed and visually sophisticated. Strong graphic symmetry overall, but allow small inconsistencies that make it feel drawn and printed by hand. The frame should feel optimistic, energetic, slightly retro, playful and empowering rather than corporate.
Only the decorative frame. The entire central area must remain completely blank warm cream, with no person, photograph, scenery or object inside it. Burnt orange dominant, cream accent, vintage graphic-print aesthetic, intricate border, hand-drawn typography, symbolic road-sign illustrations, editorial fashion-poster energy, 16:9 landscape format.

PROP SHEET — single weathered grey-blue tarp strip, three views on one frame, stylized 3D animated-film asset photography.

SUBJECT — One identical salvaged tarp panel displayed in three complementary views. A small asymmetrical strip cut and torn from a larger heavy-duty woven tarp.

Approximately 20 cm long and 11 cm wide. Irregular elongated trapezoid silhouette with one long reinforced edge, one shorter intact edge and two weathered torn edges.

The material is sturdier, thicker and more durable than lightweight plastic-film or kite fabric. It remains flexible enough to bend into a shallow curve and briefly hold air under pressure.

LEFT side of frame: FULL TOP VIEW. The tarp lies nearly flat with its complete silhouette, reinforced edge, torn perimeter, fold lines and attachment holes clearly visible.

CENTER of frame: THREE-QUARTER HERO VIEW. The identical tarp is gently draped over a low invisible support, demonstrating its weight, semi-stiff behavior and ability to form a broad aerodynamic curve.

RIGHT side of frame: SIDE PROFILE VIEW. The same tarp rests in a shallow curved shape, revealing its thickness, reinforced hem and structured material memory.

Identical object in every view, preserving the exact outline, holes, tears, seams, stains and crease pattern.

DESIGN — Heavy woven polyethylene tarp with a visible fine crosshatch grid. Base color is sturdy muted grey-blue #8A93A0.

Sun-faded raised areas use lighter blue-gray #A8AFB7. Fold recesses and overlapping fibers use darker slate-gray #66717E. Abraded edge fibers reveal small pale gray-beige marks #B7B2A8.

The color remains subdued, neutral and slightly warm-gray. It is visibly greyer and less saturated than vivid blue plastic.

SHAPE — Asymmetrical trapezoid with a broad inner end and a slightly narrower outer end.

The upper long edge is reinforced by a folded double-layer hem. Two parallel stitch lines run along this reinforced edge.

The lower edge is irregularly torn, with one shallow inward notch near the center and a short triangular section missing near the narrower outer corner.

One short end remains relatively straight and reinforced. The opposite end tapers into a rounded torn corner with several short frayed fibers.

ATTACHMENT DETAILS — Four small existing puncture holes distributed around the perimeter:

Two holes sit along the reinforced long edge.

One hole sits near the broad inner corner.

One hole sits near the narrow outer corner.

Each hole is irregularly stretched rather than perfectly circular. The surrounding weave shows mild whitening from previous tension. Hole positions remain identical across all views.

A short remnant of old gray stitching remains near one corner. No metal eyelets or manufactured fasteners.

WEATHERING — Strong beach exposure with uneven sun fading, salt residue, fine abrasion and several shallow fold lines.

One darker stain follows part of the lower torn edge. Tiny pale salt crystals remain inside selected weave recesses. Sparse embedded sand grains appear near the broad inner corner.

Three recognizable crease lines cross the panel:

One long diagonal crease from the broad inner corner toward the center.

One shorter horizontal crease near the narrow end.

One shallow curved fold across the middle.

The material remains structurally intact. The reinforced upper edge is especially strong, and the central woven area has continuous fibers despite surface wear.

MATERIAL BEHAVIOR — Semi-stiff woven plastic fabric with more weight and resistance than thin film. The panel forms broad curves rather than small fluttering wrinkles.

The reinforced edge retains its shape. The torn lower edge flexes more freely. When draped, the center sags gently while the strong upper hem holds a clean line.

The panel can stretch taut, fold, crumple and expand into a rounded air-filled shape while preserving the same identifiable outline and damage marks.

Full top view on the left, draped three-quarter view in the center and curved side profile on the right. Maintain generous spacing and preserve the complete silhouette in every view.

Behind him, a juvenile seabird sinks through the murky water. Sean turns, sees the bird and immediately rushes toward it. LOCATION PLATE — @loc_seans_hollow

A small, hidden hollow tucked into the base of a dune or beneath a rock overhang, just large
enough for Sean's body of work — private, sheltered from wind and sight, clearly his alone. Sandy
floor, packed firm from repeated use. Soft, filtered daylight reaches in from the entrance, dimmer
and cooler than the open beach outside.

THE COLLECTION — closest to the entrance, meant to be seen first

A small, carefully arranged collection of shells — not a pile, an arrangement: sorted loosely by
size and color, spaced with visible care, the kind of attention that suggests he's imagining one
specific shell he hasn't found yet rather than simply hoarding whatever he comes across.

Beside the shells, two or three small objects made from litter but elevated — handcrafted rather
than salvaged: a bottle cap polished to a soft shine and strung on a fiber like a medal; a twist
of colorful plastic wrapper woven into a small ornament; a shard of smooth, sea-worn glass
propped upright where it catches the light, displayed rather than discarded. Nothing here reads
as trash repurposed carelessly — each piece shows real, patient effort.

THE WORKSHOP — deeper into the hollow

Further back, the wing-building materials: salvaged sticks and reeds bundled and sorted by
length, scraps of tarp and fabric stretched and drying, lengths of found cord and fishing line
coiled neatly, a half-assembled wing frame leaning against the hollow's wall. Organized, not
chaotic — the workspace of someone methodical about an ambitious project, not someone
scavenging at random.

Framed so the collection and the crafted objects sit in the foreground/entrance area, naturally
catching the eye first, with the wing-building materials visible but slightly further back and
in softer focus — establishing the emotional read (he's trying to build a better life) before the
practical one (he's building wings).

them read as cared-for and distinct from the general clutter.

SCENE CONTEXT
A twenty-second stylized 3D animated sequence on a quieter section of the beach during clear later-midday light. Exactly six adult seabirds and one smaller juvenile arrive at their habitual refuge and land on one massive horizontal driftwood trunk. The adults land confidently; the juvenile is visibly still learning, flapping harder, making a cute unsteady landing, then immediately watching the adults and trying to copy their resting postures.
The sequence follows Sean along the tideline as he discovers a curved kite fragment and visually connects its shape with the birds.

<<<44fb8935-583e-4ad7-ad4f-de6a042c3aa5>>>: one massive solid horizontal driftwood trunk resting directly on sand. Long continuous gently concave upper ridge, thick weathered body, rounded uneven ends, deep horizontal grain and two dark elongated knots across its front face. Match the reference exactly. Its uninterrupted upper surface provides seven separate landing positions.
<<<d2322971-ba0d-4f63-94df-ae5feaaba4c4>>>: adult coastal seabird with off-white feathers #F2F0EB, charcoal-black wingtips #2B2B2B and warm ochre beak and feet #E8A33D. Exactly SIX adults. Match the referenced anatomy, proportions, plumage, colors and materials.
<<<37cdf9ae-00fe-4b0d-b7c1-ec026129f9d4>>>: juvenile seabird, visibly smaller than the adults. Exactly ONE juvenile. Match its referenced anatomy, proportions, plumage, colors and materials. It remains the same small bird throughout, identifiable by its scale and inexperienced movement.
<<<de65bfde-baee-4e37-ad20-f51c7e1072e6>>>: small orange hermit crab with expressive orange eyestalks and a natural stone-tan spiral shell with muted brown-grey growth bands. Dry, clean and wearing his base shell. Match the reference exactly.
: torn sun-bleached kite fragment #E6D9A8 with faded fabric stretched over a bent lightweight support, retaining a visible shallow aerodynamic curve. Match the reference exactly.
LOCATION MAP
The entire sequence takes place within the quieter natural geography of <<<98bd284e-fad6-4fb6-ab47-f11b9eba3541>>>.
The refuge occupies a dry-sand area farther up-beach. The massive trunk lies horizontally across the frame, its continuous upper ridge completely visible, with ocean and sky behind it.
Six adult landing stations are distributed along the trunk. A seventh station is reserved for the juvenile between two adults near the center-right, with enough clear wood for its small landing correction. No other bird occupies this space.
The Sean shots occur closer to the waterline, among damp sand, shallow foam, natural shells and sparse muted olive kelp.
The refuge remains geographically up-beach and screen-right. Sean travels screen-left to screen-right; his eyeline toward the birds rises upward and screen-right.
FIRST FRAME / BLOCKING
The first frame is already moving. The trunk spans almost the full width of the lower half of the composition. Its broad upper ridge is clearly readable.
Exactly six adults and one juvenile approach from the upper-left at separate heights and distances. The leading adults extend their feet toward the wood. The smaller juvenile trails slightly below and behind, already making quicker, deeper wingbeats than the adults.
Keep the juvenile unobstructed against sky throughout its approach and against clear wood during landing. Its struggle must be readable within the wide shot.
FORMAT MODE
Four shots with HARD CUTS only at 5.0s, 10.0s and 15.0s. No additional cuts or insert shots. Each segment maintains its stated framing and screen direction.
OPTICS
0.0s to 5.0s — Wide landing composition, 63° FOV. The full trunk, all seven birds and sufficient approach space remain visible. The juvenile’s wing effort, landing wobble and first imitation remain readable.
5.0s to 10.0s — Low three-quarter tracking shot of Sean, 47° FOV.
10.0s to 15.0s — Close sand-level discovery composition, 29° FOV. The kite fragment dominates the lower frame while Sean’s claws and face remain readable.
15.0s to 20.0s — Over-the-shoulder deep-focus composition, 47° FOV. Sean, the fragment and all seven birds on the distant trunk remain simultaneously legible.
FOV remains fixed within each shot. Natural motion blur accompanies wings, walking legs, falling sand and moving fabric.
CAMERA
0.0s to 5.0s — Locked camera approximately 45 cm above the sand, level with the trunk’s upper ridge and positioned on its shadow side. Bird movement creates the action. No cut or push-in to emphasize the juvenile.
5.0s to 10.0s — Camera approximately 8 cm above damp sand, tracking parallel to Sean at a three-quarter angle. Both travel screen-left to screen-right at approximately 0.4 km/h.
10.0s to 15.0s — Static camera approximately 3 cm above sand, looking toward Sean as he lifts the fragment.
15.0s to 20.0s — Locked camera immediately behind and slightly above Sean’s shell, on his shadow side. Deep focus retains the distant perch.
ACTION
0.0s to 1.0s — The first two adults descend, extend their feet and land directly on the main trunk’s upper ridge. Controlled braking strokes, a small body compression, then wings fold.
Behind them, the juvenile flaps noticeably harder and faster to maintain its approach. A brief attempt to glide costs it a little height; it immediately resumes determined wingbeats.
1.0s to 2.0s — The next two adults land at separate stations on the same ridge. One adjusts its grip; another lowers its tail for balance. The juvenile continues working behind the remaining adults, with small tail corrections and slightly uneven wing timing.
2.0s to 2.8s — The final two adults land, bringing the adult count on the trunk to six. The juvenile remains the only bird airborne. Its reserved station stays open.
2.8s to 3.6s — The juvenile approaches its station a little too eagerly. It raises its wings late, makes several quick braking strokes and extends both feet. Its toes contact the solid ridge; its body tips forward slightly with the remaining momentum.
It takes two tiny corrective steps directly along the wood, wings briefly spread and tail fanned for balance. A soft crouch absorbs the landing. It steadies itself without falling, leaving the trunk or touching another bird. The moment is endearing because of its earnest effort, not exaggerated slapstick.
3.6s to 4.2s — As soon as it has landed and steadied its feet, the juvenile turns toward the adult immediately beside it. The adult stands comfortably with folded wings and a softly lifted chest.
The juvenile studies that posture, then folds its own wings, straightens its small body and lifts its chest a little too proudly. A tiny ankle wobble interrupts the pose; it quietly corrects itself, watching the adult again.
4.2s to 5.0s — The adult relaxes its neck into a compact resting posture. A fraction of a second later, the juvenile copies the same neck tuck and body angle. It checks the adult once more, adjusts its wings and holds its small, slightly overcareful version of the pose.
All seven remain individually spaced on the same trunk. The six adults are at ease; the juvenile is visibly trying to look equally accomplished.
5.0s HARD CUT
5.0s to 10.0s — Sean is already walking screen-left to screen-right along the tideline. A shallow wash retreats through the foreground, leaving reflective sand around his feet.
His weighted shell produces a gentle side-to-side rhythm. His eyestalks remain slightly elevated. He steps around a natural shell, crosses a narrow foam trail and continues toward a pale curved object.
The waterline advances slightly into the bottom of frame and retreats. Sean remains dry above his legs and continues screen-right through the cut.
10.0s HARD CUT
10.0s to 11.2s — The kite fragment fills the lower frame, half-buried in damp sand. Sean grips it with both claws and pulls it free. Damp sand peels away and falls in small clumps.
11.2s to 12.2s — First examination: he turns the fragment toward himself and holds it still. His pupils inspect its faded surface.
12.2s to 13.3s — Second examination: he tilts it sideways, revealing its shallow aerodynamic curve. One eyestalk leans closer.
13.3s to 14.3s — Third examination: he rotates the curved edge toward sunlight. The breeze catches the fabric and lifts one corner.
14.3s to 15.0s — Sean steadies the fragment. His eyestalks begin lifting toward screen-right.
15.0s HARD CUT
15.0s to 16.4s — Sean occupies the lower-left foreground, holding the fragment low in both claws. He rotates it until its raised edge resembles a folded wing profile.
